extracted.intended_audience: playwrights, comic writers, literary theorists and students of comedy
extracted.subtask_description: Theory and practical guidance for creating comic characters and comic effects for the stage (and comic writing generally), focusing on types, observation method, and social function of laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy depicts general types (not individuality)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Comedy depicts characters, that is to say, general types... the ONLY one of all the arts that aims at the general."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast with tragedy/art that aims at the individual. Examples and titles: Le Misanthrope, l'Avare, le Joueur, le Distrait as names of whole classes; a comic poet often groups secondary characters as simplified copies to exhibit a class.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method: external observation and generalisation (inductive)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Observation is always external and the result always general."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comic observation is outward, skin-deep and averages scattered data by comparing analogous cases and extracting an essence in much the way inductive sciences group facts under laws; the comic poet relies on noticing resemblances across people rather than inner individuality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic trait must be deep-rooted yet superficial (list of desiderata)
rubrics_metrics.description: "It must be deep-rooted, so as to supply comedy with inexhaustible matter, and yet superficial, in order that it may remain within the scope of comedy; invisible to its actual owner, ... visible to everybody else, ... extremely considerate to its own self, ... troublesome to others, ... immediately repressible, ... sure of reappearing under fresh aspects, ... inseparable from social life, ... capable ... of being tacked on to all the vices and even to a good many virtues."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this checklist when designing a comic trait: make it durable enough to fuel repeated jokes but limited to the surface so it remains laughable and socially correctable; ensure it is unconscious to its owner, observable by others, socially embedded, repeatable, and flexible in expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trait must be unconscious to its owner but visible to others
rubrics_metrics.description: "Invisible to its actual owner, for the comic ever partakes of the unconscious, but visible to everybody else..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the character unaware of the ridiculous element — the laugh arises from the mismatch between self-perception and others' perception. Avoid giving the character self-aware irony that would defeat the comic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trait should be self-regarding yet harmful/annoying to others
rubrics_metrics.description: "Extremely considerate to its own self... but troublesome to others..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design comic faults that allow the character to indulge without feeling shame while creating friction or irritation for other characters/audience; this fuels corrective laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trait should be immediately repressible but reliably repeatable
rubrics_metrics.description: "Immediately repressible, so that our laughter may not have been wasted, but sure of reappearing under fresh aspects, so that laughter may always find something to do."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comedic situations should allow a social corrective (so laughter 'works') yet leave scope for the trait to reappear later in new guises — sustaining ongoing comic action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy uses repetition/multiplicity to define types
rubrics_metrics.description: "A remarkable instinct... impels the comic poet, once he has elaborated his central character, to cause other characters, displaying the same general traits, to revolve as satellites round him."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To establish a type, show several characters exhibiting the same trait in different ways (satellites) so the audience recognises a reproducible category rather than a unique oddity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vanity as the central, exemplary comic element
rubrics_metrics.description: "This mixture is vanity... it is scarcely a vice, and yet all the vices are drawn into its orbit... the one failing that is essentially laughable is vanity."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Target forms of vanity (self-admiration, social-display) when seeking broadly resonant comic material; vanity can be combined with other faults to produce both subtle and coarse comic effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of ready-made social/professional categories (the Professional Comic)
rubrics_metrics.description: "There are ready-made categories established by society itself... the various trades, public services and professions... Each particular profession impresses on its corporate members certain habits of mind and peculiarities of character..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploit occupational habits, jargons and group customs as fertile, recognisable comic types (e.g., doctors, judges, soldiers). These social categories give immediate comic recognisability and scope for satire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional vanity / solemnity as comic devices
rubrics_metrics.description: "Professional vanity... Note that vanity here tends to merge into SOLEMNITY... the more questionable an art, science or occupation is, the more those who practise it are inclined to regard themselves as invested with a kind of priesthood... this is just the illusion that lies at the root of solemnity."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray professionals who overvalue their function or adopt priest-like seriousness about dubious pursuits; this incongruity between claimed importance and practical triviality produces comedy (examples: Moliere's doctors).

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional callousness as comic trait
rubrics_metrics.description: "PROFESSIONAL CALLOUSNESS. The comic character is so tightly jammed into the rigid frame of his functions that he has no room to move or to be moved like other men."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make characters so habituated to their role that ordinary human reactions are absent or muted (e.g., the indifferent judge); contrast expected sympathy with mechanical indifference for comic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confining a profession within its own jargon produces ludicrousness
rubrics_metrics.description: "The device most in use... is to confine it, so to say, within the four corners of its own particular jargon... Judge, doctor and soldier are made to apply the language of law, medicine and strategy to the everyday affairs of life..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use translation of technical language into ordinary situations (or vice versa) to highlight absurdity; refine this by combining jargon with peculiar character traits for subtler humour (examples: Regnard, Moliere's Femmes savantes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional logic: a particular, limited logic creates comic absurdity
rubrics_metrics.description: "There is also such a thing as a professional logic... certain ways of reasoning that are customary in certain circles, which are valid for these circles, but untrue for the rest of the public."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploit clashes between a group's internal reasoning and common-sense logic to generate situational comedy; emphasise the particularity of that logic rather than generic absurdity.

rubrics_metrics.name: The comic often contains a specific kind of absurdity (not absurdity in general)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Absurdity, when met with in the comic, is not absurdity IN GENERAL. It is an absurdity of a definite kind... It is not a cause, but an effect... which reflects the special nature of its cause."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for concrete, context-rooted absurdities tied to the character's cause (e.g., Don Quixote's privileged recollection forcing 'giants' on windmills) rather than abstract or arbitrary nonsense; the comic absurd must be traceable to the character or social situation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Localise comic causes at an intermediate, socially-visible level
rubrics_metrics.description: "To penetrate too far into the personality... would mean to endanger and in the end to sacrifice all that was laughable... we must localise its cause in some intermediate region of the soul... the effect must appear to us as an average effect..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep comic explanations at a level that is neither wholly physiological nor deeply psychological; the cause should be accessible and shareable so the audience recognises it as a common, generalisable failing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy's social function: laughter as corrective and reintegrative
rubrics_metrics.description: "Its function is to convert rigidity into plasticity, to readapt the individual to the whole, in short, to round off the corners wherever they are met with... Laughter is unceasingly doing work of this kind."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design comic moments that invite corrective recognition and social re-adaptation (laughter as benign social sanction). Comedy should both please and quietly instruct or chastise, aiming for sociability rather than mere mockery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy sits between art and life and is not disinterested like pure art
rubrics_metrics.description: "So we were probably right in saying that comedy lies midway between art and life. It is not disinterested as genuine art is... By organising laughter, comedy accepts social life as a natural environment... it even obeys an impulse of social life."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or composing comedy, favour works that engage practical social norms and communal correction over detached aestheticism; comedy's primary ties are social usefulness and recognisability rather than artistic disinterestedness.
